description: How a wounded League handled Vilna, Corfu and structural weaknesses in the 1920s.
content_html:
A New Idea for International Order

One of Woodrow Wilson’s Fourteen Points called for an international organisation capable of resolving disputes peacefully before they escalated into war. The result was the League of Nations, which came into existence on 10 January 1920 when the Treaty of Versailles formally took effect. It was the first permanent intergovernmental organisation of its kind in history.

Key Fact

The League’s structure had four main bodies: the Assembly (all member states, meeting annually), the Council (great-power core with permanent and elected members), the Permanent Court of International Justice, and the Secretariat (the administrative office). Specialist commissions — including the International Labour Organisation and the Health Organisation — handled technical matters.

The Missing Members

The League began with a fundamental structural problem: the United States never joined. Despite Wilson’s central role in its creation, the US Senate refused to ratify the Versailles Treaty in November 1919 and again in March 1920. Republican senators, led by Henry Cabot Lodge, feared the League’s commitments would drag the USA into future wars without Congressional approval. American absence meant the League lacked the economic and military weight of the world’s rising superpower.

Germany was excluded from membership until 1926, when the Locarno spirit temporarily eased tensions. Russia was also absent — the Bolshevik government was not recognised by most Western states until the late 1920s, and the Soviet Union was only admitted in 1934. These absences meant the League spoke for a limited section of the world and could not act decisively when major powers defied it.

The League’s Successes in the 1920s

Despite its limitations, the League achieved genuine successes in the first decade. Its humanitarian work was wide-ranging. Fridtjof Nansen was appointed the League’s first High Commissioner for Refugees. He devised the Nansen passport — an internationally recognised identity document for stateless people — which helped hundreds of thousands of displaced persons after the First World War and the Russian Revolution. Nansen was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922.

The League’s International Labour Organisation worked to improve working conditions globally, setting minimum standards for hours, wages, and child labour. The Health Organisation (a predecessor of the World Health Organization) co-ordinated international responses to typhus outbreaks in Russia and Eastern Europe. The Slavery Commission monitored conditions in territories where the practice had not been formally abolished.

The League successfully resolved several territorial disputes that might otherwise have led to conflict. In 1921, Sweden and Finland both claimed the Aaland Islands. The League’s commission awarded them to Finland, with guarantees for the Swedish-speaking population, and both nations accepted the verdict. In 1925, the League settled the border dispute between Turkey and British-controlled Iraq over the oil-rich Mosul region, awarding Mosul to Iraq.

The Vilna and Corfu Crises

The League’s record against powerful states was less impressive. In 1920, Polish General Lucjan Żeligowski seized the city of Vilna from Lithuania with troops officially acting outside Polish command. The League condemned the action but took no practical steps to reverse it, and Vilna remained under Polish control. Lithuania refused to accept the outcome and the two countries remained in a state of formal hostility for the rest of the decade.

The Corfu incident of 1923 was more damaging. After five Italian officials surveying the Greek-Albanian border were murdered in Greek territory, Italian Prime Minister Benito Mussolini ordered the bombardment and occupation of the Greek island of Corfu. Greece appealed to the League, whose Council condemned the Italian action. However, Mussolini refused to accept League jurisdiction and threatened to withdraw Italy from the organisation. Under pressure, the League passed the matter to the Conference of Ambassadors, which ordered Greece to pay compensation to Italy — a humiliating reversal. Italy had defied the League and emerged better off.

Key Fact

The Corfu incident showed that the League could be openly defied by a major power and would back down rather than impose sanctions. Mussolini’s Italy used force, ignored the League’s ruling, and paid no penalty. This revealed a critical weakness: the League had moral authority but lacked the military force to compel obedience from powerful states.

The Geneva Protocol and Disarmament

In 1924, the League’s members drafted the Geneva Protocol, which would have committed members to submit all disputes to arbitration and to act collectively against any state labelled an aggressor. It was seen as a way to close the gaps in the League’s Covenant. However, the newly elected Conservative government in Britain refused to ratify it in 1925, citing concerns about imperial commitments, and the Protocol never came into force.

Disarmament remained an unfulfilled aspiration. The Versailles Treaty had disarmed Germany on the explicit understanding that other nations would follow. Yet France, with memories of two invasions, was unwilling to reduce its forces, and the World Disarmament Conference convened in 1932–34 ultimately failed without agreement. Germany’s resentment at being the only disarmed major power grew throughout the decade.

Historians point to several structural weaknesses that limited the League’s effectiveness beyond the 1920s crises. Decisions of the Assembly required unanimity, giving each member state an effective veto. The absence of the USA, Germany, and the USSR meant the League never represented all the major powers simultaneously. It had no standing army of its own and depended entirely on member states volunteering forces — something they were reluctant to do during economic hardship. Economic sanctions, the League’s main non-military tool, required all members to participate to be effective; partial sanctions simply shifted trade to non-participating countries. These weaknesses became fatal in the 1930s when authoritarian states openly challenged the international order.
exam_tip_html: A common error is to describe the League as a complete failure in the 1920s. Examiners reward balance: acknowledge humanitarian and technical successes (Nansen passports, ILO, Aaland) alongside political failures (Vilna, Corfu). For the Corfu incident, make sure you can explain the sequence precisely — Mussolini defied the League, the League referred the matter to the Conference of Ambassadors, and Greece had to pay compensation. The key point is not just that the League failed but why: it lacked enforcement powers and depended on voluntary participation from the states it needed to control.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The League of Nations was founded in 1920 but was weakened from the start by the absence of the USA, Germany, and the USSR, leaving it without the great-power membership needed for universal authority.
  • In the 1920s the League achieved genuine humanitarian successes (Nansen passports, ILO) and resolved smaller disputes (Aaland Islands, Mosul), but failed to act decisively when powerful states like Italy defied it (Corfu, 1923).
  • Structural weaknesses — unanimity rule, no standing army, dependence on voluntary sanctions — meant the League’s authority rested on moral persuasion rather than force, a critical limitation that became fatal in the 1930s.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which the League of Nations promoted humanitarian welfare in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each way scores 1 mark for identification and 1 additional mark for specific detail. Examples: Fridtjof Nansen devised the Nansen passport (1) helping stateless refugees from the First World War and Russian Revolution (1); the International Labour Organisation set minimum working conditions (1) including standards for hours, wages and child labour (1); the Health Organisation co-ordinated responses to typhus (1) preventing the spread of epidemic disease across Eastern Europe (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the League of Nations failed to act effectively during the Corfu crisis of 1923.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully developed with specific evidence and causal analysis (e.g. the League lacked a standing army so could not compel Italy to withdraw; Mussolini threatened to leave the organisation, which would have set a precedent of defiance, so Council members chose to back down rather than risk the League's collapse). Secure: Both reasons explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason explained, one identified. Emerging: One or both reasons named without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the United States never joined the League of Nations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple interconnected causes — isolationism in US foreign policy tradition; Republican Senate opposition led by Henry Cabot Lodge; fear of being drawn into European wars without Congressional consent; specific Senate rejection in November 1919 and March 1920. Connects these to show why not a single cause but a political coalition of concerns. Secure: Two or more causes explained. Developing: One cause explained, others listed. Emerging: General reference to the USA not joining without causal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the League of Nations' structure.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature plus 1 mark for supporting detail. Feature 1: The Assembly included all member states (1); it met annually and required unanimous decisions on major issues (1). Feature 2: The Council contained the great powers as permanent members (1); it also had rotating elected members who represented smaller nations (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Compare the following two interpretations of the League of Nations in the 1920s. Interpretation A argues the League was a genuine success, settling disputes and improving lives internationally. Interpretation B contends the League was fundamentally flawed from the start and its 1920s successes masked deeper structural failures. How far do the interpretations differ, and what might explain those differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies key differences (scale of achievement, structural vs. contextual factors); uses own knowledge (Aaland/Corfu/Nansen/US absence) to support each; explains reasons for disagreement (what evidence each selects, when the interpretation was written). Secure: Explains differences with relevant evidence from both sides. Developing: Notes some differences with one-sided support. Emerging: Summarises each interpretation without comparison.

practice_questions.text: How far was the absence of the United States the main reason for the League of Nations' weaknesses in the 1920s? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs US absence against other structural factors (unanimity rule, no army, partial membership) and specific failures (Corfu, Vilna, failed disarmament); acknowledges what the League did achieve; uses named historians or interpretive positions where relevant. Secure: Clear argument addressing both the main factor and alternatives with specific evidence. Developing: Some argument with basic evidence; may focus disproportionately on US absence. Emerging: Descriptive account with limited argument. SPaG: 5 marks.

knowledge_checks.q: Which crisis saw Italy bombard a Greek island and face no effective League penalty?
Why did the US Senate refuse to join the League of Nations?
options: Senators feared it would commit the USA to foreign wars without Congressional consent
The USA had already joined a rival organisation

knowledge_checks.q: Fridtjof Nansen devised the _____ passport to help stateless refugees after the First World War.
The 1924 _____ Protocol, which would have strengthened the League by requiring arbitration, was never ratified.
Match each League of Nations body to its function.
right: Set minimum standards for working conditions

flashcard_questions.q: When was the League of Nations founded?
flashcard_questions.a: 10 January 1920, when the Treaty of Versailles came into force

flashcard_questions.q: Why did the USA not join the League of Nations?
flashcard_questions.a: The US Senate refused to ratify the Versailles Treaty, fearing loss of sovereignty in foreign wars
An internationally recognised identity document created for stateless refugees by Fridtjof Nansen

flashcard_questions.q: What happened during the Corfu incident of 1923?
flashcard_questions.a: Italy bombarded and occupied Corfu; the League backed down and Greece paid compensation to Italy

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Vilna crisis of 1920?
flashcard_questions.a: Polish troops seized Vilna from Lithuania; the League condemned it but took no action

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Aaland Islands settlement show about the League?
flashcard_questions.a: The League could successfully resolve disputes between smaller powers in the 1920s

flashcard_questions.q: Why did the Geneva Protocol of 1924 never come into force?
flashcard_questions.a: Britain refused to ratify it in 1925, citing concerns about imperial commitments

flashcard_questions.q: What structural decision-making weakness limited the League's Council?
flashcard_questions.a: Major decisions required unanimity, giving any member an effective veto

flashcard_questions.q: Which three major powers were absent from the League in the 1920s?
flashcard_questions.a: The USA, Germany (until 1926), and the USSR

flashcard_questions.q: What was the League's main non-military enforcement tool?
flashcard_questions.a: Economic sanctions — but these required all members to participate to be effective

glossary_terms.definition: An international organisation founded in 1920 as part of the Versailles settlement, designed to maintain peace and encourage cooperation between nations.
Norwegian explorer appointed High Commissioner for Refugees by the League in 1921, known for introducing the Nansen passport for stateless refugees.
A Swedish-speaking archipelago between Sweden and Finland whose sovereignty was disputed after the First World War; awarded to Finland by the League in 1921.
A 1924 proposal to strengthen the League by making all signatories submit disputes to arbitration and respond collectively to aggression; it was never ratified.
